lesson.title: Splitting a Limit in Two: The Sum Rule
lesson.summary: The sum rule says that if two functions each settle down to a specific number as x approaches a point, then their sum settles down to the sum of those two numbers, which lets you evaluate complicated limits piece by piece.
lesson.body:
When a quantity settles down to a fixed value as x gets close to some point a, that settling behavior is remarkably stable under addition. If f(x) is squeezing in on a number L, and g(x) is squeezing in on a number M, then f(x) plus g(x) has to be squeezing in on L plus M. This is not a coincidence you have to take on faith. If f(x) can be forced within any tiny distance of L by choosing x close enough to a, and g(x) can be forced within any tiny distance of M the same way, then f(x) plus g(x) can be forced within the sum of those tiny distances of L plus M, just by choosing x close enough to a to satisfy both conditions at once.

This is the Sum Rule for Limits, one of the core limit laws: if the limit of f(x) as x approaches a equals L, and the limit of g(x) as x approaches a equals M, with L and M both real numbers, then the limit of f(x) plus g(x) as x approaches a equals L plus M. The rule requires both individual limits to exist and be finite. Running the same argument with a minus sign gives the closely related difference rule: the limit of f(x) minus g(x) equals L minus M.

Here is a worked example. Let f(x) equal x squared and g(x) equal 3x minus 1, and find the limit of f(x) plus g(x) as x approaches 2. Handle each piece on its own first. The limit of x squared as x approaches 2 is 4, since values like 1.9 squared equal 3.61 and 2.01 squared equal 4.0401 close in tightly on 4. The limit of 3x minus 1 as x approaches 2 is 5, since that line passes directly through the point (2, 5) with no gap or hole. By the sum rule, the limit of x squared plus 3x minus 1 as x approaches 2 equals 4 plus 5, which is 9. Check this against the combined function directly: h(x) equals x squared plus 3x minus 1, and h(2) equals 4 plus 6 minus 1, which is 9. The two methods agree.

The real payoff of the sum rule is that it lets you break an intimidating expression into small, separately manageable pieces, evaluate each piece on its own, and recombine the results. The rule extends naturally to three or more functions added together, since you can apply it repeatedly: the limit of f plus g plus h equals the limit of f, plus the limit of g, plus the limit of h, one addition at a time.

One caution matters here. The sum rule only applies when each piece individually has a finite limit. Consider the limit as x approaches 0 of 1 over x, plus negative 1 over x. The combined expression simplifies to 0 for every x not equal to 0, so its limit is clearly 0. But neither 1 over x nor negative 1 over x has a limit at 0 on its own, since both grow without bound. You cannot legally invoke the sum rule to split this limit apart; you have to simplify algebraically first, and only then evaluate. That ordering question, simplify first versus split first, is exactly the kind of judgment call that later algebraic limit techniques train you to make.

The sum rule is the first member of a small family of algebraic limit laws, all following the identical pattern: evaluate the limits of the individual pieces, then combine them using the same operation that combined the pieces originally. The product rule, quotient rule, constant multiple rule, and power rule, covered next, all extend this same idea to multiplication, division, scaling, and exponents.
